d: You twist what the other person said, then argue against the twisted version instead of the real one.
x: Straw Man Ask yourself: is this reply about what was actually said, or about a bigger, worse version of it? Phrases like “So what you’re saying is…” are often a sign the argument just got stretched. Bring it back to the original, calmly: “That’s not what I said. I said a little less, not never.” And don’t start defending a position you never took. “Maybe we eat out a little less this month.” — “So you want us to sit at home and never have any fun?!” Someone posts that e-scooters need clearer parking rules downtown. Top reply: “So you want to ban scooters and make everyone drive?” A caller says the team should rest its star player more. The host fires back: “Oh, so you want him sitting on the bench all season?”

d: You attack the person instead of answering what they said.
x: Ad Hominem Check whether the reply is about who said it or about what was said. If the argument itself is left standing with no answer, that’s a dodge. “Maybe I am all those things. That doesn’t change whether these numbers are right or wrong. Can we talk about the numbers?” “You’re going to lecture me about spending? You can’t even save $50!” — The actual question was whether this purchase is too much. “Ignore him, he’s a loser who can’t even hold a job.” — posted as a reply to a thread full of numbers and sources. “That idea came from the new hire, so obviously they don’t get how things work here.”

d: You present just two options as if they’re the only ones, when there are plenty of others.
x: False Dilemma When you hear “it’s either this or that,” ask: Is there a third option? A middle ground? A chance both are wrong? “It doesn’t have to be one or the other. There’s also this, and this. Can we look at all of them?” “Either you get into a top-ten college, or you’re going to end up with nothing.” “You’re either with us, or you’re a traitor.” “Buy today at this price, or regret it for the rest of your life.”

d: You treat an idea as true because lots of people believe it or do it.
x: Appeal to Popularity If the only reason offered is “everyone,” there’s still no evidence for the idea itself. “Sure, a lot of people do it. But what’s the reason it’s actually right?” “Every kid in her class got a smartphone at eight, so that must be the right age.” “This post has 100,000 likes, so what it says has to be true.” “Over a million Americans have switched!” — The number doesn’t tell you whether it’s right for you.

d: We look for information that backs up what we already believe, and ignore or downplay what goes against it.
x: Confirmation Bias Ask yourself: what evidence would change my mind? If you can’t name any, the opinion probably came before the evidence. With yourself: go looking, on purpose, for the strongest case against your view and read it carefully. With others: “Let’s look at the evidence against our side too.” You’re convinced your neighbor is rude, so you remember every time he didn’t wave back — and forget the time he jumped your car. You only follow accounts that agree with you, so it feels like “everyone” sees things your way. You’ve already decided on a certain car, so you read only the glowing reviews and wave off the bad ones as “probably fake.”

d: The first number we hear pulls our judgment of every number after it, even when it has nothing to do with anything.
x: Anchoring Ask: if I hadn’t heard that number, what would I have guessed this was worth? And try to set your own number before you hear anyone else’s. Do your research and walk in with your own number. If someone throws out a number that’s way off, say: “Let’s start from what the market actually pays.” The seller says, “It’s $80, but for you, $50,” and you feel like you scored. It might really be worth $30. They show you the fully loaded trim first, so when you see the next one down, its price suddenly looks reasonable. Whatever salary number gets said first in a negotiation shapes the whole conversation after it.

d: You treat a claim as true because someone important or famous said it, even if they’re not an expert on that topic.
x: Appeal to Authority Ask two questions: Is this person actually an expert in this specific subject? And do other experts in the field agree? “With respect, he’s an expert in X, not in this. What do people who study this say?” “Your uncle the engineer says that medication doesn’t work.” — Your uncle is an engineer, not a doctor. “That actor says this coin is going to the moon, so I have to buy in.” A famous quarterback tells you this shampoo makes your hair stronger.

d: You treat something as right because “we’ve always done it this way.”
x: Appeal to Tradition If the only reason is “we’ve always done it” or “that’s just how it’s done,” nobody has said yet why it’s actually good. “It might be a great tradition. But what does it actually do for us? And if we find a better way, can we try it?” “We’ve always bundled babies up in heavy blankets, even in July. You think you know better than Grandma?” “We’ve done this spreadsheet by hand for ten years. Why change it now?” “A wedding has to be done this way. That’s just how people do it.”

d: You try to win someone over by stirring up their feelings instead of giving them a real reason.
x: Appeal to Emotion Strip the feelings out and look at what’s left: is there a logical reason? Or is it just pressure on your emotions? “I get that this is moving. But let’s look at the reasons. Why is this the right choice?” “If you really loved me, you’d buy me this phone.” “Share if you have a heart. Anyone who scrolls past is cold as ice.” A commercial packed with sad piano music and teary kids that ends with: “Upgrade your phone plan today.”

d: You treat something as good or safe because it’s “natural,” or bad because it’s “artificial.”
x: Appeal to Nature Remember that poison ivy is natural, arsenic is natural, and plenty of lab-made medicines save lives. “Natural” is not evidence. (And none of this is medical advice — talk to a doctor before stopping any medication.) “Natural versus artificial isn’t the real question. The question is: is there evidence it helps and doesn’t hurt?” “These herbs are natural, so there’s no way they can hurt you.” A wellness influencer: “Ditch your meds and try this natural remedy instead.” “100% natural” printed on a bottle with zero information about what it actually does.

d: You dismiss advice or criticism because the person giving it makes the same mistake.
x: Tu Quoque Notice when the reply is about the person’s behavior, not about whether the point is true. A point can be right even if the person making it doesn’t live by it. “Fair — I do that, and I shouldn’t. But that doesn’t make the point any less true.” Dad: “Smoking is bad for you.” Teen: “You smoke!” — Smoking is still bad for you. “You’re telling me not to be late? You were late yesterday.” “You’re posting about littering when I literally saw you toss a cup out your car window once.”

d: You switch to a different topic to get away from the original question.
x: Red Herring Go back to the original question and ask: did the reply actually answer it? If it went somewhere else entirely, that’s a red herring. “We can talk about that later. But first: what’s the answer to my question?” “Where did the whole paycheck go?” — “Well, why don’t you ever make the food I like?” The manager asks why the project is behind, and the employee starts talking about how swamped the other department is. A reporter asks about the service outage, and the spokesperson gives a long speech about the company’s awards from years ago.

d: You claim one small step will inevitably lead to disaster, without showing that each step will actually cause the next.
x: Slippery Slope Count the steps between the start and the disaster, and ask about each one: what’s the evidence this will happen? If there isn’t any, it’s just fearmongering. “Okay, let’s take this step and set a clear limit. If what you’re worried about starts happening, we revisit.” “If we let him stay up until 11 tonight, tomorrow it’ll be 3 a.m., then he’ll drop out of school, and his whole future is ruined.” “If we allow one work-from-home day, nobody will ever work again and the company will go under.” “Today it’s one inflatable lawn decoration. Tomorrow the whole street looks like a carnival!”

d: You assume one thing caused another just because it happened before it, or alongside it.
x: Post Hoc / False Cause Ask: could a third factor be causing both? And does this happen every time, or was it a coincidence? “Maybe. But it could also be this other thing. How would we figure out which one is the real cause?” “I wore this jersey and my team won, so it’s my lucky jersey.” “Ever since they put up that cell tower, people around here keep getting sick. It has to be the tower.” “Sales went up after we changed the logo color.” — Maybe it was the holiday season, or a promotion.

d: You draw a conclusion about everything from just one or two examples.
x: Hasty Generalization Ask: how many examples is this judgment based on? And do those examples really represent the whole group? “That may have happened. But is one time really enough to judge all of them?” “We ordered from that store once and it broke in a week. Everything they sell is junk.” “I met two people from Boston and they were both rude. Everyone from Boston is like that.” “The new hire made one mistake in a report. Guess they just can’t do the job.”

d: You use the conclusion you’re trying to prove as evidence for itself, so you just go in a circle.
x: Begging the Question Take the conclusion out and see: is there any other evidence left? If the evidence is just the conclusion in different words, you’re going in circles. “That’s the same claim said another way. What’s the evidence from outside the claim?” “I’m right because I don’t make mistakes.” “This page is trustworthy, because it says it only posts the truth.” “This plan is the best one, because there’s no plan better than it.”

d: A question with an accusation or assumption built in, so any direct answer admits the assumption.
x: Loaded Question Before you answer, look for what the question is assuming. Has that actually been established? Don’t answer yes or no. Answer the assumption: “That question assumes I was lying, and I wasn’t.” “Have you stopped lying to me?” — Say yes or no, and you’ve admitted you were lying. “Why is the city ignoring the pothole problem?” — before anyone has shown that it is. “When are you going to stop holding up the project?”

d: You use the same word in two different senses within one argument to reach a false conclusion.
x: Equivocation When a key word shows up in an argument, ask: does it mean the same thing every time it’s used? “Let’s agree on this first: what exactly do you mean by that word?” “The doctor said fast food is heavy, and this burger is tiny, so it’s fine.” — The doctor meant hard on your body, not heavy on a scale. “Light” on the label — light in weight? In calories? In color? In flavor? “Germ theory? It’s just a theory, and a theory is just a guess.” — In science, a “theory” is an explanation backed by a large body of evidence, not a guess.

d: When an example breaks your claim, you redefine the group to push that example out, instead of admitting the claim was too broad.
x: No True Scotsman Notice when someone adds “real” or “true” right after an example contradicts them. It usually means they’re protecting the claim from being wrong. “What exactly makes someone ‘real’? If the definition changes every time we find a counterexample, the claim isn’t saying anything anymore.” “A real man never asks for directions.” — “My dad asks all the time.” — “Then he’s not a real man, is he?” “No true fan ever boos their own team.” — “Plenty of fans boo.” — “Those aren’t real fans.” “Midwesterners are all nice.” — “My neighbor from Ohio is a jerk.” — “Well, he’s not a real Midwesterner.”

d: You make a claim, then demand that others prove it wrong instead of proving it right yourself.
x: Shifting the Burden of Proof Ask: who made the claim first? The person making a claim is the one who owes the evidence. “You’re the one who said it, so the evidence is on you. Show me what made you say that.” “This car has a problem.” — “What problem?” — “You prove to me it doesn’t.” “This supplement cures everything, and if you don’t believe me, prove it doesn’t.” “That guy is leaking info to competitors, and if you don’t believe me, prove he isn’t.”

d: You treat something as true because nobody has proven it false, or false because nobody has proven it true.
x: Appeal to Ignorance If the only evidence is “nobody proved otherwise,” then we simply don’t know yet. Not knowing isn’t evidence for anything. “The fact that nobody’s disproven it means we don’t know yet — not that it’s true. Let’s wait for real evidence.” “Nobody’s proven this house isn’t haunted, so it must be haunted.” “Scientists haven’t been able to prove this remedy doesn’t work, so it works.” “Nobody has complained about the new system, so everyone must love it.” — Maybe people just don’t know where to complain.

d: You treat one personal experience or story as stronger evidence than data and studies.
x: Anecdotal Evidence Ask: is this one person’s experience, or is there data on lots of people? The story might be true, but it doesn’t represent everyone. “Good for Grandpa, honestly. But that’s one person. What do the numbers say about thousands of people?” “Grandpa smoked his whole life and lived to 90, so smoking can’t be that bad.” “My cousin tried this cream and her skin cleared up, so it’s the best cream out there.” “I hired one person from that college and they were terrible, so none of their grads are any good.”

d: You show only the evidence that supports your side and hide the evidence against it.
x: Cherry Picking Ask: is this everything there is, or just a piece of it? What might have been left out? “Okay, those are the good examples. Can we see the full picture, including the parts that don’t help our case?” “9 out of 10 customers are satisfied!” — without saying how many they asked or how they chose them. A restaurant’s website shows three glowing reviews and leaves out the hundred one-star ones. A report highlights the one month when sales were high and skips the months when they dropped.

d: You compare two things that are alike in one way and conclude they must be alike in another, unrelated way.
x: False Analogy Ask: are these two things alike in the specific way we’re talking about? Or are they alike in some completely different way? “It’s a nice comparison, but there’s an important difference: this. So the conclusion doesn’t have to be the same.” “Kids are like houseplants. Just leave them alone and they’ll grow.” — But kids need raising, not just water and sunlight. “We’re a family here, so a good employee doesn’t complain about unpaid overtime.” “Running a city is just like running your household budget — if you’re in debt, you sell the furniture.” — A city’s finances don’t work like a family’s checking account.

d: You reject something because it’s hard for you to imagine or understand, not because there’s evidence it’s wrong.
x: Personal Incredulity If the reason is “I just can’t believe it” or “it doesn’t make sense to me,” that describes your feeling, not the thing itself. “I’m surprised too, but surprise isn’t evidence. Let’s figure out how it actually works.” “How can a plane that weighs hundreds of tons just float in the air? Something doesn’t add up.” “There’s no way my phone knows where I am with GPS turned off. That’s a lie.” “No way this software does the whole job in a minute. They’re fudging the numbers.”

d: You judge an idea as right or wrong based on where it came from, not on what it actually says.
x: Genetic Fallacy Ask: if the exact same idea came from a different source, would I accept it? If yes, I’m judging the source, not the idea. “Okay, let’s set the source aside and look at the idea itself: is it right or wrong?” “That idea came from some tech bro in Silicon Valley, so it can’t be any good.” “That was reported by a news site I can’t stand, so it’s obviously fake.” “Our competitor came up with that process, so we’re not using it.”

d: You assume that what’s true of the parts is true of the whole, or the other way around.
x: Composition / Division Ask: does this quality really carry over from the part to the whole, or from the whole to the part? Or is the whole something different from the sum of its parts? “Each piece is great on its own, but that’s no guarantee they’ll be great together.” “We just signed five All-Stars, so we’re guaranteed to be the best team in the league.” — A team of stars might not play well together. “I love every one of these ingredients, so the dish is going to be delicious.” “That company is hugely successful, so every single person who works there must be brilliant.”

d: Believing a random event is “due” because it hasn't happened in a while, or won't happen because it just did.
x: Gambler's Fallacy Ask: is each try independent of the last one? A coin has no memory of how it landed last time. “Each try stands on its own. The odds don't shift because of what happened before.” “We've had three girls, so the next one's definitely a boy.” — The odds are still roughly 50/50. “This number hasn't come up in months. It's got to hit soon.” “This ref has given us a bunch of penalties lately, so the next close call has to go our way.”

d: Assuming the truth must sit halfway between two positions, even when one of them is flat-out wrong.
x: Argument to Moderation Ask: how much evidence does each side actually have? If one side has none, the middle isn't the answer. “Meeting in the middle is great for negotiating, not for facts. Let's look at what the evidence says.” “Your cousin says the Earth is round, your uncle says it's flat. The truth is probably somewhere in the middle.” “The engineer says the bridge needs 100 tons of steel, the contractor says 50. Let's split it at 75.” — 75 might not hold the bridge up. A segment seats a doctor next to a wellness influencer and presents their views on vaccines as two equally supported sides.

d: Sticking with a losing bet because of what you've already put in, not because it's worth continuing.
x: Sunk Cost Fallacy Ask: if I hadn't spent anything yet, would I start this today? What's spent is gone. The only question is what comes next. “That money's gone whether we keep going or stop. The question is: what's the best move from here?” “We paid $16 a ticket. We're sitting through this terrible movie to the end.” “I've already sunk $5,000 into repairs on this car, so I have to fix it again.” — Even if the repair now costs more than the car is worth. “We've spent a year on this project. We can't stop now.” — Even when it's clearly not going to work.

d: Answering a criticism by pointing at someone else's wrongdoing instead of addressing the criticism itself.
x: Whataboutism If the reply starts with “What about...” and names someone else, ask: did the original criticism actually get answered? “Maybe they're wrong too, and we can talk about that later. Right now we're talking about this.” “Why is your room such a mess?” — “What about my brother's room? It's way worse!” “This company's customer service is awful.” — “What about the other company? They're even worse!” “That was a dirty hit by our guy.” — “What about their linebacker last week?”

d: Rejecting an idea entirely because the argument for it contains a fallacy, even though the idea itself might be true.
x: Fallacy Fallacy Remember: a weak argument means that particular reason isn't enough. It doesn't mean the claim is false. Better evidence may still exist. “Agreed, that argument is weak. But that doesn't prove the idea is wrong. Let's look for better evidence.” “You told me not to smoke because Uncle Mike said so. That's an appeal to authority, so smoking must be fine.” “This ad is pure emotional manipulation, so the product has to be junk.” “Your point is a hasty generalization, so everything you said is wrong.”

d: Judging how common or dangerous something is by how easily examples come to mind.
x: Availability Heuristic Ask: am I seeing this a lot because it's actually common, or because it's recent and keeps showing up in front of me? Reach for numbers instead of memory: “What do the statistics actually say?” After seeing news coverage of a plane crash, you feel more nervous about flying than driving, even though the drive is far riskier. Every day there's a new post about a stolen package, so it feels like the whole area has gotten unsafe, even if the numbers say otherwise. At review time, the manager remembers your most recent slip-up and forgets a full year of solid work.

d: Letting one good trait, like looks or fame, make us assume everything else about a person is good too.
x: Halo Effect Ask: am I judging this specific thing, or am I being swayed by some other trait that has nothing to do with it? Rate each quality on its own. Make a list: experience, price, quality, and give each a separate score. The candidate is polished and charming, so the interview breezes by and nobody really digs into their experience. A beloved actor promotes a payday-loan app called QuickCashly, and people assume the app must be legit. The star of the basketball team gets a little extra leniency when the teacher grades his English essay.

d: Our tendency to do or believe something because lots of people around us do.
x: Bandwagon Effect Ask: if nobody else were doing this, would I still do it? Take a minute before you act, and write down your own reason, not the crowd's. You see a long line outside a store and join it before you even know what they're selling. A new trend takes off, everyone's doing it, so you do it too without asking whether it actually fits you. Everyone you know piled into the same new coin, so you buy in too, afraid of missing out.

d: The sting of losing something tends to feel bigger than the joy of gaining something of the same value.
x: Loss Aversion Ask: am I rejecting this because it's actually a bad decision, or because I don't want to feel the loss? Look at the whole decision: “If I didn't already own this, would I buy it today at this price?” Losing a $20 bill bugs you a lot more than finding a $20 bill on the sidewalk makes you happy. “Don't miss out on this deal” tends to hit harder than “Get a discount,” even though they mean the same thing. A stock keeps dropping, and you won't sell because that would mean admitting the loss, so you lose even more.

d: The exact same information can lead us to different decisions depending on how it's worded.
x: Framing Effect Flip the wording in your head: if the same thing were said the opposite way, would I feel the same about it? Convert everything into full numbers in the same format, then compare. “This surgery has a 90% success rate” sounds more reassuring than “10% of these surgeries fail,” even though it's the same number. Ground beef labeled “95% lean” sells better than the same beef labeled “5% fat.” “Just $15 a day” sounds lighter than “$450 a month.”

d: After something happens, we feel like we saw it coming all along, and that it was obvious.
x: Hindsight Bias Ask: did I actually say or write that prediction before it happened? If not, my memory may be rearranging itself. Write your predictions down before things happen, then check back later. You'll be surprised. After the game: “I knew they'd lose the second I saw the starting lineup.” “It was obvious that marriage wasn't going to last.” — Said after the divorce. “That project was clearly doomed.” — Nobody said so before it failed.

d: When someone else messes up, we blame their character and overlook the circumstances. When we mess up, we see the circumstances right away.
x: Fundamental Attribution Error Ask: if I had done the exact same thing, how would I explain it? Before you judge someone, think of three circumstances that could be behind what they did. The car ahead cuts you off: “What a reckless jerk.” When you cut someone off: “I was running late.” Your coworker joins the meeting late: “So unprofessional.” You join late: “Traffic was brutal.” Your kid didn't study: “He's just lazy.” Nobody asks whether he was sick or something was bothering him.

d: Our tendency to believe, back, and give more chances to people from our own group, like our hometown, team, school, or family.
x: In-group Bias Ask: if someone from the other group did exactly the same thing, would I judge them the same way? Swap the names in your head and see whether your verdict changes. When your team's player makes a hard hit, it's “playing tough.” When the other team does it, it's “dirty.” The manager keeps handing opportunities to people from his alma mater without realizing it. Bad news about someone from your hometown: “Must be fake.” The same news about someone from the rival town across the river: “Typical.”

d: Preferring that things stay the way they are, even when a change would be better for us.
x: Status Quo Bias Ask: if I were choosing from scratch today, would I pick this? Put a reminder on your calendar every few months to review the things you never revisit, like plans and streaming subscriptions. Your phone plan is overpriced and doesn't fit how you use it, but you keep it because you're “used to it.” A new tool would cut the team's busywork in half, but nobody wants to try it. Your savings have sat for years in an account that pays next to nothing, because switching feels like a hassle.

d: Believing bad things are less likely to happen to us than to other people.
x: Optimism Bias Ask: if a friend said this about themselves, would I believe them? And what happened the last few times? For deadlines and budgets, take your estimate and add a buffer, because most people lowball. “I'm a good driver, I'm not going to crash.” — So you text while driving. “This project will take a week.” — And it takes a month, like every time. “That stuff happens to other people.” — So you keep putting off your annual checkup.

d: Bad things affect us more and stick in memory longer than good things of the same size.
x: Negativity Bias Ask: am I holding on to this because it actually matters, or just because it was negative? Write down the good things too, so you're looking at the whole picture. Ten customers thanked you today and one complained, and on the drive home all you can think about is the complaint. Bad news tends to spread faster and get more engagement than good news. One harsh word in an argument stays with you for years, while plenty of kind words fade.

d: Looking only at the people or things that made it, and forgetting the ones that tried the same thing and failed, because they're no longer visible.
x: Survivorship Bias Ask: where are the people who tried the same thing and failed? And how many of them are there? “Okay, that's a success story. But out of every 100 people who tried this, how many made it?” “That founder dropped out of college and became a billionaire, so college is pointless.” — Nobody talks about the thousands who dropped out and didn't make it. “Old furniture was built to last, not like today.” — The old stuff that fell apart got thrown out. Only the good pieces are left. Videos titled “How I made a million day trading.” The people who lost money don't make videos.

d: Believing other people notice our appearance and our mistakes far more than they actually do.
x: Spotlight Effect Ask: do I remember other people's slip-ups in this much detail? Probably not, and neither do they. Remember that everyone is busy with themselves and the spotlight they feel on them. There's a small coffee stain on your shirt, and you feel like everyone's staring at it all day. You stumbled over one sentence in your presentation and replayed it for a week. Nobody else remembered. You hold off on posting because “what will people think,” when most of them will scroll past in a second.

d: Adding a third option nobody would really pick can make one of the original two look much better.
x: Decoy Effect If there's an option no sensible person would choose, ask why it's there. Then mentally remove it and compare the rest. Compare only the options you're actually considering, based on what you need, not on the third option. Small popcorn is $5, medium is $8.50, large is $9. The medium is there to make the large look like a steal. Basic is $10, Premium is $15, and “Standard Plus” is $14.50 with fewer features than Premium. The third plan is the decoy. A mid-level trim is priced just below the top trim, so the top one suddenly seems “worth the difference.”

d: Our tendency to obey or believe anyone who looks authoritative, like a uniform, a title, or a position, without thinking it through.
x: Authority Bias Ask: am I convinced because the argument is good, or because this person looks important? Ask politely: “Can I ask what your background is in this?” or “What's the source?” Someone in a hi-vis vest with a clipboard asks to come in and “check the meter,” and you let him in without asking who he's with. A wellness account puts “Dr.” in front of its name, and people trust its health tips, even though the degree isn't in medicine. The boss pitches a bad idea in the meeting, and nobody pushes back.

d: Being more sure of what we know and what we estimate than our actual accuracy justifies.
x: Overconfidence Ask: how many times have I felt this sure and turned out wrong? And what could make me wrong this time? Instead of “I'm sure,” say “I'm about this sure.” And get a second opinion before big decisions. In surveys, most drivers rate themselves as more skilled than most other drivers, which can't be true for most of us. “I'm 100% sure that number is right.” — Then someone double-checks, and it's wrong. “I really understand the market.” — So he puts his entire 401(k) into a single stock.

d: The idea that people who know little about a subject overestimate their skill in it. But the evidence for the famous version of this idea is disputed.
x: Dunning–Kruger Effect This isn't a tool for judging other people. Use it as a question for yourself: how much do I really know about this? Don't use the name as an insult in an argument. Focus on the evidence in what the person says, not on their level. Someone watched two YouTube videos about economics and now argues with economists in the comments, totally confident. A new hire thinks the job is easy and the veterans just don't get it, until they dig in a little deeper. That famous chart with “Mount Stupid” and the “Valley of Despair” doesn't appear anywhere in the original study.

d: After we choose something, we remember its upsides more and forget its downsides, to convince ourselves we chose right.
x: Choice-Supportive Bias Ask: if I'd picked the other option, would I be seeing these same upsides in it? Before you choose, write down the pros and cons of each option. After you choose, go back to that list. Once you drive it off the lot, you notice every feature you love, and any flaw becomes “no big deal.” You left one job for another, and now you only remember the bad parts of the old one, even things that never bothered you. You picked a school for your kid, and now you can't stand to hear any criticism of it.

d: Setting a condition for being convinced, then changing it to something harder once it's met, instead of admitting the point.
x: Moving the Goalposts Remember the condition that was set at the start. If every time it's met a new, harder one appears, the conclusion was probably decided before the evidence. Agree on the condition up front and write it down: “What exactly would change your mind?” If it's met, calmly point back to it. “Get straight A's and you can have a new phone.” — He gets straight A's. — “No, that was just the first semester. Wait till the end of the year.” “Show me proof.” — Here's a study. — “That one's tiny.” — Here's a big one. — “Somebody must have paid for it.” “If the app gets 100 sign-ups in a month, we keep funding it.” — It gets 120. — “No, we really needed 500 for it to count as a success.”

d: Treating two things as equal because they share one feature, even though they differ hugely in size or seriousness.
x: False Equivalence Ask: are these two things really equal, or do they just share one trait? Where's the difference in size and harm? “Sure, both are wrong. But a $5 mistake isn't a $5,000 mistake. Let's keep each one in proportion.” “You forgot to pick up milk, and I forgot to pay the rent. So we're even.” “The guy who showed up five minutes late to practice is the same as the guy who shoved the ref. They both broke the rules.” A segment treats a long wait at an urgent care clinic and a ring selling counterfeit pills as “the same problem.”

d: Applying a rule to everyone else while exempting yourself or your group without a convincing reason.
x: Special Pleading Ask: what's the real difference between this case and the others? If the only reason for the exception is “me” or “us,” it's special pleading. “Maybe you do have a real reason. Tell us, and if it's convincing, it applies to everyone, not just you.” “No phones at dinner.” — A minute later, Dad takes a call: “That's work, it's different.” A driver leans on the horn at someone double-parked, then double-parks in the same spot himself: “It's just for a minute.” The manager docks pay for any lateness, but when he's late: “My situation is different. I have responsibilities.”

d: Focusing on the details in front of us and forgetting how common the thing is in the first place.
x: Base Rate Neglect Before you judge, ask: out of every 100 people, how many have this to begin with? If you don't know that number, your judgment is missing a piece. Turn percentages into head counts: “Picture 1,000 people. How many are actually sick, and how many will get a wrong result?” And try the Probability Tree game on this site. A test always catches the disease if you have it, but it also comes back falsely “positive” for 5% of healthy people. You test positive for a rare disease that affects 1 in 1,000 people, and you panic. But picture 1,000 people: 1 is actually sick, and about 50 healthy people also test positive. So most positive results here are false alarms. (This is an illustration, not medical advice. Ask your doctor what your own results mean.) “Most car crashes happen close to home, so your own neighborhood is the real danger!” — Well, most of your driving happens close to home in the first place. “He's quiet and loves reading, so he's probably a librarian.” — Even though accountants outnumber librarians many times over.

d: After any really extreme result, the next one is usually closer to normal. When we forget that, we invent a reason for the change.
x: Regression to the Mean (Neglect) Ask: was the last result extreme? If yes, the change that followed may be perfectly normal, not caused by whatever we did. “Before we say it was X, let’s look at every month, not just the best or worst one.” And if you can, compare with a group that didn’t do the same thing. A rookie running back rushes for 200 yards one Sunday, then 40 the next. “The fame got to his head.” Or that first game was just a freak outlier. A manager chews out an employee after his worst month ever, and the next month is better. So the manager concludes that yelling gets results. “My headache was at its absolute worst, I tried the tea a wellness influencer swears by, and it went away.” The headache was probably going to ease up on its own.

d: We underestimate how much time and money our own projects will take, even when every past project took longer.
x: Planning Fallacy Ask: the last three times I did something like this, how long did it actually take? If your estimate is shorter than all of them, you’re probably in planning-fallacy territory. Don’t ask “When will I be done?” Ask “How long do things like this usually take?” Then add a cushion of time and money. “The kitchen remodel will take two months, done way before Thanksgiving.” Six months later, it’s still going and the budget has doubled. “I’ll get through all the reading in the two days before the final.” The night before the exam, you realize you’re only halfway. “The report will be ready Thursday.” This is the third week in a row you’ve said that.

d: We believe a very general description is about us specifically, even though it fits almost anyone.
x: Barnum Effect (Forer Effect) Ask: could this fit my friend, my sister, or a random person on the bus? If yes, it isn’t saying anything about me. Try reading the same description to someone else without telling them where it came from. If they say “That’s so me,” the description is vague, not accurate. “What your favorite color says about you”: “You’re kind, but nobody really gets you.” So you share it and write, “This is literally me!” The horoscope column: “This week brings some pressure, but you’ll find a way through.” That fits anyone, any week. A team offsite runs a “personality test,” and the result says: “You love people, but you also need time to recharge.” Everyone in the room feels seen.

d: We see something as more valuable and more desirable just because it’s rare or the deal is about to end.
x: Scarcity Effect Ask: if there were plenty of these and no deadline, would I still buy it at this price? Give yourself a day before any big purchase. And if the salesperson says “It’ll be gone,” you can calmly say: “If it’s gone, it wasn’t meant for me.” “Only 3 left in stock!” So you bought a jacket you weren’t even planning to get. “We’ve only got two left at this price, and prices go up on the first.” So you signed today without checking a single other dealership. An ad says: “24 hours only!” A week later, the same deal is still running.

d: A group cares more about staying in agreement than about getting the decision right, so nobody pushes back.
x: Groupthink If a decision sailed through fast with zero objections, ask: is that because the idea is genuinely good, or because nobody wanted to be the odd voice out? Before deciding, ask someone to play devil’s advocate on purpose, or have everyone write down their view privately before the most senior person speaks. The boss pitches an idea in the meeting and everyone says “Love it.” Afterward, people DM each other on Slack: “That idea is going to flop.” The whole family is excited about your sister’s new fiancé. Everyone has a concern about him, but nobody wants to be “the one who ruins it.” The friend group chat plans a Vegas trip. Anyone who asks about the budget gets “Why are you always such a buzzkill?” So they stop asking.

d: When we succeed, it’s because we’re good. When we fail, it’s because of the circumstances or other people.
x: Self-Serving Bias Compare how you explain your wins with how you explain your losses. If success always comes from you and failure always comes from outside, there’s a bias at work. Privately, after any failure ask, “What part of this was in my control?” And after any success ask, “What outside help did I get?” “I aced it because I studied hard.” And in the class you failed: “The professor is unfair and the exam was impossible.” When your team wins: “We played great.” When it loses: “The refs robbed us.” When the deal closes: “I closed it.” When it falls through: “Accounting held up the paperwork.”

d: If you have more than one explanation for the same thing, start with the one that needs the fewest assumptions.
x: Occam's Razor When you catch yourself building a long story with lots of assumptions to explain something ordinary. Or when you have several explanations and don’t know where to start. Write down the explanations in front of you and count how many “ifs” each one needs to be true. Test the one with the fewest first. If it fails, move to the next. Your phone won’t charge. Before you decide the motherboard is fried, try a different cable and clean out the charging port. That’s usually the problem, and it costs nothing. A coworker hasn’t answered your email. Maybe they’re upset and ignoring you… or it landed in spam. Start with the simple question: “Did my email come through?” A post in the neighborhood Facebook group claims the Wi-Fi keeps dropping because “someone on our street is jamming the network on purpose.” The simpler explanation: the router needs a restart or there’s an outage with the provider, which you can check in two minutes.

d: Don’t explain someone’s behavior with bad intent if a slip, a mistake, or simply not knowing is enough to explain it.
x: Hanlon's Razor When you feel hurt or wronged by something someone did, and the first explanation that pops into your head is “They meant it.” Especially if they have no history of bad intent. Ask yourself: is there an innocent explanation that fits? If so, start there. And instead of an accusation, ask a question: “Did you realize that…?” Your roommate ate the last slice of cake you were saving. Instead of “They did it to mess with me,” maybe they just didn’t know it was yours. The barista got your order wrong. During the morning rush, they probably misheard you, not picked you out to annoy. Repeat it nicely instead of starting a fight. Your manager left your name out of the team thank-you email. Before deciding “They don’t see me,” consider that they may have been rushing and sent it from their phone. Remind them kindly.

d: Present the other person’s view in its strongest, best form, and only then respond to it.
x: Steelmanning Before any discussion with a real disagreement, or when you find yourself thinking the other side’s view is “dumb” or “makes zero sense.” That usually means you haven’t understood it yet. Restate their view in your own words until they say, “Yes, that’s exactly what I mean.” Look for their strongest reason, not their weakest. Only then start responding. Your parents want you to major in nursing instead of film. Instead of “You don’t get it,” you say: “You’re worried about me ending up in an unstable career, and you want me to be secure. Right?” Then you make your case. A coworker is against the new plan. Before you respond, you sum up their objection: “You think the timeline is tight, the team is already stretched, and this plan will break us.” If they say “Exactly,” now you can actually discuss it. Your buddy thinks the coach should be fired. Instead of mocking him, you say: “The results have been bad for months and there’s no clear identity to the team. I get it.” Then you explain why you think the coach deserves another shot.

d: Break a problem down to the basic facts you’re sure of, and build the solution from there instead of copying “what everyone usually does.”
x: First-Principles Thinking When the ready-made solutions aren’t working or cost too much, or when the only answer you have is “That’s just how it’s done.” Also when you’re starting something new and don’t want to just copy everyone else. Ask: what’s the real goal here? Which things am I sure are true, and which are just habit or assumption? Strip out the assumptions and build the solution from the facts that remain. “Everyone at work swears by a $15-a-month budgeting app.” Break it down: what do I actually need? A set amount saved by a certain date, without touching it before then. Maybe the app helps, or maybe an automatic transfer to a separate savings account every payday does the job for free. The AC is running up your electric bill, and the standard advice is “Buy a new unit.” Go back to basics: where is the heat getting in? Maybe blackout curtains on the window that gets the afternoon sun solve half the problem. “We’ve always had a standup every morning.” The first-principles question: what is this meeting for? If the goal is that everyone knows the updates, maybe a Slack post is enough three days a week.

d: Instead of asking “What should I do to succeed?” ask “What would guarantee I fail?” and steer clear of it.
x: Inversion When the goal is big and you can’t tell where to start, or when you keep collecting “how to succeed” tips and nothing changes. Sometimes it’s easier to know what to avoid than what to do. Write down the goal. Flip it: “How would I guarantee the opposite?” List every route to failure. Mark the ones you’re actually doing right now, and start there. Want to save? Ask: how could I make sure my paycheck is gone in a week? Order DoorDash every night, shop online at 1 a.m., and never track a single expense. That’s exactly the list to avoid. Want a better relationship with your dad? Ask: what damages it the most? Arguing at dinner, snapping back, and only calling when I need something. Start by stopping those. Before a client pitch, ask: what would make this pitch a disaster? A dead laptop, mistakes in the numbers, showing up late. Now you know what to prep the night before.

d: Don’t stop at the first consequence of a decision. Ask: “And then what?”
x: Second-Order Thinking In decisions with long-lasting effects: money, parenting, rules at work or at home. Especially when the solution looks “easy and comfortable” right now. Once you’ve named the first consequence, ask “And then what?” two or three more times. Think about the other people involved: how will they react when this happens? And compare: better today, or better a year from now? Buy now, pay later on a new TV: $40 a month feels like nothing. That’s the first effect. And then? Two years of payments, possible fees if you miss one, and less wiggle room if something comes up. You hand your kid the tablet so they’ll stop whining, and it works. And then? They learn that whining gets the tablet, so tomorrow they whine more. You say yes to every extra project to keep your boss happy. And then? It becomes what’s always expected of you, the quality slips, and you burn out.

d: Don’t remove a rule or an old practice until you first know why it was put there.
x: Chesterton's Fence When you want to scrap a rule, change a system, or remove something that looks pointless. Especially if you’re new to the place. Ask: who put this here, and why? What problem was it solving? If you find the reason and it no longer applies, remove it with a clear conscience. If you can’t find it, dig a little first. Your grandma checks every stove knob before bed, and you think it’s an old habit. Before you drop it, ask her why. Maybe there was a scare with a burner left on once. There’s an extra review step on invoices that looks like a waste of time. Before you cut it, ask the person who had the job before you. Maybe it was added after a mistake that cost the company a lot. Residents want to take down the gate around the pool because it’s “annoying.” Before anyone calls a contractor, someone should ask the property manager: why was it installed, and when?

d: Hold your view with a level of confidence, and raise or lower it based on how strong each new piece of evidence is, instead of all-or-nothing.
x: Bayesian Updating When new information reaches you about something you have an opinion on. Or when you notice yourself flipping 180 degrees with every headline, or the opposite: never budging no matter what happens. Before the evidence: how sure am I? (Say, 60%.) After it, ask: how likely would this evidence be if I’m right, and how likely if I’m wrong? If the gap is big, move your view a lot. If it’s small, move it a little. You hear there might be layoffs. That rumor goes around every year and usually doesn’t happen, so your worry starts low. Then you notice leadership holding a lot of closed-door meetings: you raise your worry a bit and update your résumé, but you don’t quit. Your kid gets a bad grade on one test. On its own, that doesn’t mean they’re “slacking.” If it happens in several subjects over several months, then the picture really changes. A TikTok says gas prices are about to spike next month. One video is weak evidence, so you nudge your view a little. If an official source confirms it, you move it a lot.

d: Decide up front what evidence would make you admit you’re wrong.
x: Falsifiability Test When you’re extremely sure about something, or someone offers you a claim that no possible result could ever prove wrong. And in any argument that’s going around in circles. Ask yourself or the other person: “What would I have to see to say I’m wrong?” Write it down before you start looking. If there’s no answer, the view needs a second look, or it isn’t the kind of view that can be debated at all. Your friend says, “The new coach is a bust.” You ask: what could convince you he’s good? If the answer is “Nothing,” that’s not an opinion you can test or debate. It’s a fixed position. Someone is selling you a course that will “make you rich.” You ask: what result, if it doesn’t happen in three months, would tell me it doesn’t work? If the answer is always “You just didn’t apply it right,” the claim can’t be tested. You’re convinced late-night phone use is why your kid’s grades dropped. You set the test: if we turn the phone off at 10 p.m. for a month and nothing improves, I’m wrong and I’ll look for another cause.

d: Before you start a plan, imagine it has already failed, and ask: “Why did it fail?”
x: Premortem Before any plan involving money, time, or lots of people. Especially when everyone is excited and nobody wants to be “the one who rains on the parade.” Sit down with the group (or by yourself) and say: “It’s six months from now, and the plan failed badly.” Everyone spends a few minutes writing reasons on their own. Read them out, then pick the top three to deal with now. Before your sister’s wedding: “Imagine the wedding was a mess. Why?” One person says the venue opened late; another says the photographer has no backup if they cancel. Now you can fix those things ahead of time. Before launching an ad campaign: “It’s a month from now and the campaign flopped. What happened?” Someone says we targeted the wrong audience; someone else says the budget ran out in a week. Now you have a real list of risks. Driving to the beach for the weekend: “Imagine the trip was a disaster.” A flat tire, no gas station on a long stretch of highway, the Airbnb canceled. So you check the tires and confirm the booking the day before.

d: Judging an idea true or false because its outcome would be good or bad, not because of the evidence.
x: Appeal to Consequences Separate two questions: “Is this true or not?” and “Do I like what follows from it?” If your answer to the first comes from the second, you’re looking at an appeal to consequences. “I get that the outcome would be hard, but that’s not evidence it isn’t true. Let’s find out first, and then figure out how to deal with it.” “If the test shows something, it’d be a disaster, so there’s definitely nothing wrong.” And so they never get the test done. “If that crypto platform turns out to be a scam, I’ve lost my life savings. So there’s no way it’s a scam.” “If that catch gets overturned, we’re out of the playoffs. So it was obviously a catch.”

d: Painting the target after you shoot: grabbing a slice of data that happens to show a pattern, ignoring the rest, and saying “See? Not a coincidence.”
x: Texas Sharpshooter Fallacy Ask: was this pattern defined before we looked at the data, or picked out afterward? And where’s the rest of the data that didn’t make it into the story? “Let’s set the prediction first, then test it on new data. If the pattern is real, it’ll show up again.” After the season ends, a fan digs through the team’s results until he finds they won every game played on a Thursday, and posts: “Thursday is our day. Not a coincidence.” He had no prediction about Thursdays before he went looking. “Three people on our street have the same illness. It must be the cell tower on that roof.” Nobody checked whether that number is actually unusual for how many people live there. A video: “The numbers in your birthday hold a secret!” It collects every number that matches and stays quiet about every one that doesn’t.

d: Rejecting a good solution because it isn’t perfect, by comparing it to an ideal solution that doesn’t exist.
x: Nirvana Fallacy (Perfect Solution Fallacy) When you hear “But that won’t solve the whole problem,” ask: compared to what? Is this solution better than what we have now or not? “Right, it’s not perfect. But the question isn’t whether it’s perfect. The question is whether it’s better than what we’ve got.” “Seatbelts don’t save everyone in a crash, so what’s the point?” “The new system still has bugs, so let’s go back to paper.” And paper has way more problems. “If I can’t save $500 a month, I’m not going to save at all.”

d: We value something more just because it’s ours, so we ask more for it than we’d ever pay to buy it.
x: Endowment Effect Ask: if this weren’t mine and I saw it for sale, what would I pay? If that number is way below what I’m asking, that’s the endowment effect. Look at what similar items actually sold for, not just asking prices. And have someone with no attachment to it estimate the price for you. “My car is worth $18,000.” Every listing and trade-in offer says about $14,500, but you’re sure they “just don’t get it.” You list your used phone on Facebook Marketplace and get annoyed when someone haggles. Yet you haggle on every used phone you buy. Your closet is full of clothes you haven’t worn in years, but every time you go to donate them, they feel “still perfectly good.”

d: We see something as better and more valuable when we put effort into making it ourselves, even if it’s ordinary or worse than the store-bought version.
x: IKEA Effect Ask: if someone else had made the exact same thing, would it look this good to me? Get feedback from someone who didn’t see the effort behind it. And at work, if you can, evaluate ideas without the owners’ names attached. You cooked a new recipe for the first time, it came out just okay, and you can’t figure out why the family isn’t as excited as you are. You spent three days shooting and editing a video, and you don’t get why it’s doing worse than one you threw together in 15 minutes. You defend the idea you sweated over with everything you’ve got in the meeting, even when a coworker’s idea is simpler and better.

d: We like something more just because we’ve seen or heard it a lot, even without paying attention to it.
x: Mere-Exposure Effect Ask: do I like this because it has a real advantage, or just because I’m used to seeing it? When choosing between two options, write down the pros of each on paper. And remember: an ad that runs over and over isn’t convincing you, it’s getting you used to it. A commercial jingle you never really noticed is suddenly stuck in your head a month later, and at the store your hand goes straight to that brand. A creator you didn’t know or care about shows up in your feed twenty times, and now you watch their videos to the end. A new coworker you weren’t sure about, and after two months of sitting next to them you actually like them, without anything special happening.

d: We remember an experience by its most intense moment and by how it ended, not by the whole thing or how long it lasted.
x: Peak–End Rule Ask: am I judging the whole experience, or just its strongest moment and its ending? Try to remember the ordinary stretch in the middle. Before deciding whether to repeat an experience or avoid it, remember it from start to finish. And if you provide a service, care about the ending, but don’t let it cover up a problem in the middle. The day at the beach was crowded and hot the whole time, but it ended with ice cream on the boardwalk, so on the drive home everyone says, “What a great day.” A customer waited on hold for half an hour, but the rep solved the problem kindly at the end, so they gave the service five stars. The team looked awful for eight innings, then hit a walk-off home run, and everyone leaves the stadium saying, “What a game.”

d: Once you know something well, it’s hard to imagine someone else not knowing it, so you explain it as if they already do.
x: Curse of Knowledge Ask: if I didn’t know this yet, would I understand what I just said? If there’s a word an ordinary person wouldn’t know, the curse of knowledge is probably at work. Explain it to someone outside the topic and ask them to say it back in their own words. And use an everyday example instead of the technical term. The teacher says “This part is obvious” and skips three steps in the problem, and the whole class is lost. You send a client an email full of phrases like “Q3 roadmap,” “KPIs,” and “circling back on the deck,” and they have no idea what you want from them. You’re showing your dad something on his phone: “Tap here, then here,” way too fast, and you get frustrated that he isn’t following.

d: We think we can influence things that are actually up to chance or outside our control.
x: Illusion of Control Ask: if I didn’t do this at all, would the outcome actually be different? Do I have evidence, or is it just a feeling? Separate what’s in your hands from what isn’t, and put your time and money into the first. If your rituals make you happy, keep them, just don’t bet money on them. “I’ll pick my own lottery numbers instead of a Quick Pick. That way my odds are better.” The drawing is random either way. You sit in the same spot on the couch and wear the same jersey every game so your team will win. You press the elevator button five times in a row, as if that will make it come faster.

d: We want to believe people get what they deserve, so when something bad happens to someone, we tend to look for a mistake they made that explains it.
x: Just-World Belief If you catch yourself asking “What did they do to deserve this?” before “How can I help?”, pause. And ask: could this have happened to anyone in their place? Start with empathy and help. Questions about causes can come later, framed as “How do we prevent this?” not “Who do we blame?” And if someone is blaming the victim, calmly say: “This could happen to any of us.” Someone gets their phone snatched on the subway, and instead of helping, people say: “Well, why did you have it out in a crowd?” A coworker is let go in a round of layoffs, and you hear: “They must have been slacking on something.” Even though the cut hit the whole department. A post about someone who got scammed, and the top comments are: “Serves them right for being greedy.” Before anyone even asks how the scam worked.

d: We think most people think and choose like we do, more than they actually do.
x: False Consensus Effect Ask: do I have numbers showing people are like me, or is it just my feeling? And the people I talk to, are they like everyone, or like me? Ask people who are different from you before you decide. At work, run a quick poll or test with a small sample before assuming. You made an ad that fits your own taste and figured “Everyone will love it like I do.” Then the engagement came in weak. “Who even eats this without hot sauce? Everybody likes it spicy.” And you’re the only one in the house who does. “I love working late, so I’m sure the whole team is fine with a 9 p.m. call.” Nobody was asked.

d: The man who walked around the marketplace asking people questions until they realized they didn't know what they thought they knew.
x: Socrates Athens, c. 470–399 BCE Socrates never wrote a single word. Everything we know about him comes from his students, mainly Plato. His method was to ask: “What is courage? What is justice?” Every time someone answered, he asked another question that showed the definition had a hole in it. The goal wasn't to win the argument. The goal was for both people to understand the thing better. He's credited with the idea that the first step toward wisdom is knowing that you don't know. Your friend says, “Dave's a good guy.” You ask, “What makes someone a good guy?” He says, “He coaches Little League and never swears.” You ask, “What if someone never swears but quietly stiffs his contractors?” Now your friend is actually thinking about what “good guy” means. That's the Socratic method.

d: He believed what we see with our eyes is only shadows, and that the real thing lives in a world of unchanging Forms that we reach through reason.
x: Plato Athens, c. 427–347 BCE Plato was Socrates' student and wrote down his dialogues. His most famous image is the Allegory of the Cave: people chained in a cave since childhood see only shadows on the wall and take them for reality. If one of them got out and saw the sun, he'd realize everything he knew was an illusion. And if he went back to tell the others, they'd laugh at him or hurt him. Plato also founded the Academy, one of the first great schools in history. Someone who spends every evening scrolling Instagram starts to believe everyone else's life is beach trips, brunch and promotions. Those posts are the shadows on the cave wall. Real life, the part off-camera, looks very different.

d: “The First Teacher”: the first to lay out the rules of logic, and the thinker who saw virtue as a middle point between two extremes.
x: Aristotle Greece, 384–322 BCE Aristotle wrote about nearly everything: logic, ethics, politics, biology, poetry. He was the first to set down the rules of the syllogism: if all humans are mortal, and Socrates is a human, then Socrates is mortal. In ethics, he argued that a virtue sits between two vices: courage between cowardice and recklessness, generosity between stinginess and wastefulness. The philosophers of the medieval Arabic-speaking world called him “the First Teacher.” One guy puts every group dinner on his credit card to look generous and can't make rent. Another guy has never picked up a check in his life. Neither one is generous. Generosity means giving in the right place, in the right amount.

d: He said the goal of life is happiness, but for him happiness meant peace of mind, not partying.
x: Epicurus Greece, 341–270 BCE His name became shorthand for indulgence, which is unfair to him. Epicurus lived very simply: bread, water and friends. His idea was that most of our unhappiness comes from unnecessary desires and from fear, especially fear of death. He sorted desires into three kinds: natural and necessary, like food; natural but not necessary; and empty ones, like fame and piles of money. Someone picks up extra shifts so he can upgrade to the newest phone every year, and never has time to hang out with his friends. Epicurus would tell him: you're paying with the most valuable things you own, your time and your peace of mind, for an empty desire.

d: The physician-philosopher whose medical textbook was taught in Europe for centuries, and who asked: if you were created floating in midair with no sensations at all, would you still know you exist?
x: Avicenna Bukhara and Hamadan, 980–1037 CE Avicenna, known in Arabic as Ibn Sina, was born near Bukhara in Central Asia and worked across Persia. He wrote The Canon of Medicine, which was used in European universities into the 1600s, and The Book of Healing, a huge work of philosophy. His most famous thought experiment is the “Floating Man”: imagine a person created suddenly in midair, eyes closed, touching nothing, not even feeling his own body. Avicenna argued that this person would still know he exists. In other words, self-awareness comes first. It doesn't come from the senses. When you sit alone in the dark and hear your own thoughts, you know you exist without needing any outside evidence. Avicenna was trying to catch that moment and understand it.

d: The scholar who doubted everything he knew in order to find certainty, and wrote about his crisis of doubt with rare honesty.
x: Al-Ghazali Tus and Baghdad, 1058–1111 CE Al-Ghazali was one of the most celebrated scholars of his time in Baghdad when he fell into a crisis of doubt. In his autobiography, Deliverance from Error, he describes asking: how can I trust my senses, when my eye sees a star as tiny even though it's bigger than the Earth? And how can I trust reason itself? He reached total doubt before finding his way out through Sufism, a mystical, experience-based path. In The Incoherence of the Philosophers he criticized thinkers like Avicenna, and he also argued that the link between cause and effect, like fire and burning, is something we see out of habit. We never actually observe a necessary connection. You're sure that pressing the elevator button brings the elevator, because you've done it a thousand times. But you've never actually seen the link between the button and the elevator. You've seen one thing happen after another. Al-Ghazali noticed this about 600 years before David Hume did.

d: The judge and philosopher who explained Aristotle to the world, and argued that careful reasoning and religious belief don't have to be enemies.
x: Averroes Córdoba and Marrakesh, 1126–1198 CE Averroes, known in Arabic as Ibn Rushd, was a judge, physician and philosopher in Muslim Spain (al-Andalus). His commentaries on Aristotle were so thorough that medieval Europe simply called him “the Commentator.” In The Decisive Treatise he argued that rational inquiry isn't opposed to religion, because truth cannot contradict truth. He answered Al-Ghazali in The Incoherence of the Incoherence. His ideas had a huge influence on European thought, and a whole movement there, Latin Averroism, was named after him. If someone tells you, “Don't overthink it, thinking just makes things worse,” Averroes would answer: thinking is a tool. The problem isn't the tool. It's using it badly.

d: One of the first people to ask why states rise and fall, and to insist that a historian should question a report before passing it on.
x: Ibn Khaldun Tunis and Cairo, 1332–1406 CE Ibn Khaldun was born in Tunis, served many North African courts, and spent his last years in Cairo as a judge. In his Muqaddimah (“Introduction”) he did something new: instead of just telling history, he tried to find its patterns. His best-known idea is asabiyyah, or group solidarity: a group bound by strong ties can build a state, but after a few generations comfort and luxury loosen those ties, and the state falls. He also criticized historians who repeated impossible stories without asking: could this really have happened? Grandpa starts a hardware store from nothing and works himself to the bone. His son grows it into a chain. The grandson, who grew up with everything, runs it into the ground. Americans have a saying for this, “shirtsleeves to shirtsleeves in three generations,” and it's close to Ibn Khaldun's idea.

d: He decided to doubt everything he possibly could, and found one thing he couldn't doubt: that he was thinking.
x: René Descartes France, the Netherlands and Sweden, 1596–1650 Descartes wanted a rock-solid foundation for knowledge. So he said: I'll doubt my senses, because they fool me. I'll doubt that I'm awake, because I might be dreaming. I'll even doubt arithmetic. But there's one thing I can't doubt: that someone is doing the doubting. That's where his famous line comes from: “I think, therefore I am.” He also gave us the coordinate system you used in algebra class, which is why it's called the Cartesian plane. You wake up from a very realistic dream and need a few seconds to be sure you're actually awake. That's the same question Descartes started with: how do I know this isn't a dream right now?

d: He pointed out that the sun rising every day so far isn't logical proof it will rise tomorrow, and that we live by habit more than by reason.
x: David Hume Scotland, 1711–1776 Hume was an empiricist: all our knowledge comes from experience. But when he looked closely at experience, he found a problem. We see things happen one after another, but we never see the “cause” itself. Expecting the future to be like the past is habit, not logic. This is called the problem of induction. He also wrote that reason is “the slave of the passions,” meaning we decide with our feelings and then reason shows up with the justifications. A turkey gets fed every morning at 9 a.m. Day after day, it concludes that food arrives at 9 a.m. Then comes the week before Thanksgiving. The example came after Hume, but it captures his point perfectly.

d: He said the right thing to do is whatever you could accept as a rule for everyone, and that a person is always an end in themselves, never just a means.
x: Immanuel Kant Germany (Prussia), 1724–1804 Kant tried to bring the rationalists and the empiricists together. He argued that the mind isn't a blank slate: it organizes experience through built-in frameworks like space, time and causation. In ethics he gave his famous rule, the categorical imperative: act only on a principle you could accept as a universal law. If everyone lied whenever it was convenient, lying itself would stop working, because nobody would believe anybody. He also said: always treat people as ends in themselves, never merely as tools for your goals. You're in a hurry, so you want to cut the line at the coffee shop. Ask Kant: if everyone in a hurry cut the line, would there even be a line? No. So it's wrong.

d: The philosopher who challenged people to re-examine every value they inherited, and to live a life they'd be glad to repeat forever.
x: Friedrich Nietzsche Germany, 1844–1900 Nietzsche wrote in a style closer to poetry than to textbook prose, which is why he's so often misunderstood. He believed modern people had lost the foundation they used to build their values on, and needed to face that with courage instead of sliding into nihilism. One of his ideas is the “eternal recurrence”: if you had to live your exact same life again, and again, a million times, would you be thrilled or horrified? He also wrote that if you have a “why” to live for, you can bear almost any “how.” Someone lives to please his parents, his neighbors and his coworkers, and has never once asked himself what he actually wants. Nietzsche would tell him: you inherited those values. Test them before you live by them.

d: Separate what's in your control from what isn't, and spend your energy only on the first.
x: Stoicism Greece and Rome, from the 3rd century BCE Stoicism was founded in Athens by Zeno of Citium and named after the Stoa, the painted porch where its followers met. Its best-known voices include Epictetus, a formerly enslaved man who became a teacher, and Marcus Aurelius, a Roman emperor. The core idea: some things are up to you, like your opinions, your choices and your reactions. Other things aren't, like traffic, the weather and what people think of you. Unhappiness comes from clinging to the second kind. You're stuck in traffic on the freeway and you're going to be late for work. The traffic isn't up to you. What is up to you: sending your boss a quick message, calming down, and putting on a podcast worth hearing. Leaning on the horn won't clear the road.

d: Hold off on judging until the evidence is strong enough, and don't rush to say “definitely.”
x: Skepticism From Pyrrho in ancient Greece to today Ancient skeptics like Pyrrho believed every argument has an equally strong argument against it, so the wise move is to suspend judgment and find peace in that. Later, thinkers like Al-Ghazali and Descartes used philosophical doubt as a tool for reaching certainty. Today, “scientific skepticism” simply means: don't accept a claim without evidence that matches the size of the claim. Someone posts in the family group chat that “celery juice on an empty stomach cures high blood pressure for good.” A skeptic won't say it's a lie, and won't say it's true. A skeptic asks: where's the evidence, and who tested it? (And for anything health-related, the person to ask is a doctor, not the group chat.)

d: Reason is the main source of knowledge, and some things can be known without testing them.
x: Rationalism Europe, 17th century Rationalists like Descartes, Spinoza and Leibniz thought the senses can deceive us, and that the most solid knowledge is what we reach through reason alone, like mathematics. You don't need to measure every triangle on Earth to know its angles add up to 180 degrees in the geometry you learned in school. Their big debate was with the empiricists, who argued the opposite. If someone tells you, “I've got a square circle,” you don't need to see it to know it's impossible. Your mind figured that out on its own. That's an example of knowledge from reason.

d: Everything we know comes from experience and the senses; the mind starts as a blank slate.
x: Empiricism Britain, 17th and 18th centuries John Locke said the mind is born like a blank slate, and experience is what writes on it. George Berkeley and David Hume came after him and pushed the idea further. Empiricism is the grandparent of the scientific method: don't claim something until you've tested it and seen it. But Hume showed that if you take empiricism all the way, you run into hard problems, like the problem of induction. You'll never know what a mango tastes like from a description, no matter how good the description is. You have to taste it. That's the heart of empiricism.

d: The right action is the one that brings the greatest good to the greatest number of people.
x: Utilitarianism Britain, late 18th and 19th centuries Jeremy Bentham and John Stuart Mill argued that morality isn't a set of fixed rules; it's a calculation. Which outcome reduces suffering and increases happiness for everyone affected? This idea sits behind many decisions in public health and public policy. Mill added that some pleasures are higher than others, like the pleasure of understanding something compared with the pleasure of a good meal. A county has one budget: build one big hospital downtown, or ten small clinics in rural towns? A utilitarian asks: which choice saves more lives?

d: Don't only ask “What should I do?” Ask “What kind of person do I want to be?”
x: Virtue Ethics From Aristotle to today Instead of Kant's rules or the utilitarians' math, virtue ethics focuses on character. A good person is someone who has built good habits, like courage, honesty, generosity and fairness, until they become part of who they are. Just as you learn to drive by driving, you learn courage by doing small brave things every day. The approach came back strongly in the 20th century with philosophers like Elizabeth Anscombe and Alasdair MacIntyre. You don't become honest overnight just because you decided to. You become honest by telling the truth about small things a hundred times, until lying starts to feel strange to you.

d: Governments and laws exist because people agreed, at least implicitly, to give up a little freedom in exchange for safety.
x: Social Contract Europe, 17th and 18th centuries Thomas Hobbes argued that without government, life would be a “war of every man against every man,” so people hand their freedom to a strong authority that protects them. John Locke said people have natural rights, like life, liberty and property, and that a government that fails to protect them can rightly be replaced. Jean-Jacques Rousseau wrote about the “general will.” In the 20th century, John Rawls revived the idea with his thought experiment, the “veil of ignorance.” A four-way stop: each of us gives up the freedom to roll through whenever we feel like it, in exchange for not getting T-boned. It's a tiny social contract we live out every day.

d: Nobody is going to hand you a ready-made meaning for your life. You're free, and you're responsible for what you do with that freedom.
x: Existentialism Europe, 19th and 20th centuries It began with Kierkegaard and Nietzsche and became famous with Jean-Paul Sartre and Simone de Beauvoir in France. Sartre summed it up as “existence precedes essence”: a paper knife is designed for a specific purpose before it's ever made, but a human being exists first and then defines who they are through their choices. That freedom brings anxiety, because you can't hand the responsibility to anyone else. “My parents picked my major.” An existentialist would say: okay, but you chose to stay in it for four years, and you're the one who'll choose what to do after graduation.

d: We search for meaning, and the universe stays silent. The answer isn't despair; it's to live fully awake anyway.
x: Absurdism France, 20th century Albert Camus said “the absurd” is the clash between our hunger for meaning and the silence of the universe. He saw three possible responses: escape from life itself, escape into a ready-made answer without thinking it through, or rebel and live with passion despite the absurd. Camus chose the third. His example was Sisyphus, condemned to push a boulder uphill forever, and he concluded: “One must imagine Sisyphus happy.” Same commute, same cubicle, same small talk every day. Camus wouldn't tell you to quit. He'd tell you that you can choose to see each day with fresh eyes, and that choice is itself a kind of rebellion.

d: The meaning of an idea is the difference it makes in practice. If it makes no difference, arguing about it is a waste of time.
x: Pragmatism United States, late 19th century It was founded by Charles Sanders Peirce, William James and John Dewey. Their idea: instead of arguing about abstractions, ask what would change if the idea were true. How would you act differently? William James told the story of a camping-trip argument about a squirrel clinging to one side of a tree trunk while a man circles the tree trying to see it. Did the man “go around” the squirrel? James showed that the whole fight was about what “around” means. Two roommates argue: is it better to study in the morning or late at night? A pragmatist says: try each for a week, and whichever one helped you remember more is the better one for you.

d: Do right and wrong change from one society to another, or are some things wrong everywhere and always?
x: Moral Relativism From the Greek Sophists to today Relativists say there's no single moral standard for all humans; what's right is whatever your society considers right. The idea starts from a real observation: customs vary enormously between cultures. But there's an important difference. That people disagree about morality is a descriptive fact. That there's no right or wrong at all is a much bigger philosophical claim. In some countries eating with your hands is rude; in others it's perfectly normal. That's a difference in customs. But could torturing a child for fun ever be “right” anywhere? That's where most people feel relativism hits its limits.

d: A scientific theory is one that could be proven wrong. A theory that explains everything explains nothing.
x: Falsifiability (Karl Popper) Karl Popper, 20th century Karl Popper asked: what separates science from things that just look like science? His answer: science doesn't prove anything true once and for all. Science makes predictions that could turn out wrong. If a prediction fails, the theory falls. But a theory that can find an explanation for any result, and could never possibly be wrong, isn't science, no matter how convincing it sounds. Your horoscope app says, “This week you'll face challenges, but you'll get through them.” Whatever happens to you will seem to fit. That's not because the horoscope is accurate. It's because it can't possibly be wrong.

d: Called “the Second Teacher” after Aristotle, he believed a good city is one whose purpose is the happiness of the people who live in it.
x: Al-Farabi Farab, Baghdad and Damascus, c. 870–950 CE Al-Farabi was born in Central Asia, spent most of his life in Baghdad, and died in Damascus. He cared deeply about logic, and said logic is to reason what grammar is to language: a set of rules that protects you from mistakes.
