In The Opinions of the People of the Virtuous City, he compared a city to a human body: every organ has a role, and the whole thing works toward one goal, happiness. Such a city needs a leader with wisdom and knowledge, not just power. Its opposites are the “ignorant cities,” whose only goal is money, or pleasure, or domination. Your HOA: if every homeowner only thinks about their own house, the pool stays broken and the common areas fall apart. Al-Farabi would say the neighborhood is a “small city” that needs a shared goal and someone competent to run it, not whoever sends the angriest emails.

d: He wrote the story of a child growing up alone on an island who reaches life's biggest questions through his own reasoning and observation.
x: Ibn Tufayl Al-Andalus and Marrakesh, early 12th century–1185 CE Ibn Tufayl was a physician and court official for the Almohad rulers in Marrakesh, and he's the one who introduced Averroes to the caliph. His best-known work is a philosophical novel, Hayy ibn Yaqzan (roughly “Alive, Son of Awake”): a boy raised by a gazelle on an island with no other people. When the gazelle dies, he opens her body to find out what had kept her alive. Through observation and trial and error he learns about fire, animals and the stars, and eventually reasons his way to questions about the origin of the universe. The story asks: can a human reach knowledge through reason alone? It was translated into Latin in 1671 and spread across Europe. A kid takes the TV remote apart, piece by piece, to see how it works. His parents yell at him, but he's doing exactly what Hayy did: asking a question and going after the answer with his own hands.

d: Known as “the Dean of Arabic Literature,” he applied methodical doubt to inherited tradition and fought to make education a right for everyone.
x: Taha Hussein Minya, Cairo and Paris, 1889–1973 Taha Hussein, one of modern Egypt's most influential writers, lost his sight as a small child in a village in Minya, south of Cairo. He studied at the traditional al-Azhar university, then at the new Egyptian University, and later in France. From Descartes he took the idea of starting your research by doubting everything you've been told until evidence proves it. He applied this in On Pre-Islamic Poetry (1926), asking whether poems credited to the pre-Islamic era, before the 7th century, were really that old, or were composed later. The book caused a huge uproar, and he revised and republished it as On Pre-Islamic Literature. In The Future of Culture in Egypt he argued that education is the foundation of a nation's progress. As Egypt's minister of education in 1950, he became known for the line “education is like water and air,” and free public education was expanded. Someone shares an inspirational quote on Facebook with “— Mark Twain” underneath. Taha Hussein would ask: says who? Which book, which letter? Or is everyone just passing it along? A huge share of the quotes credited to famous people online have no known source at all.

d: The Egyptian philosopher who argued that any sentence you can't check by experience has no meaning at all, and later went back to his own heritage looking for what was still useful.
x: Zaki Naguib Mahmoud Damietta, Cairo and London, 1905–1993 Zaki Naguib Mahmoud earned his PhD in London and came home a passionate logical positivist. The idea: a sentence has meaning only if you can check it by experience, like “water boils at 212°F at sea level,” or if it's true by definition, like “a square has four sides.” A statement that no possible experience could confirm or refute isn't false; it's empty of meaning. He laid this out in The Myth of Metaphysics (1953). Later, in Renewing Arab Thought (1971), his tone changed: he argued for keeping the parts of the Arab intellectual tradition that support scientific thinking and setting aside the parts that don't. An ad for a bracelet from a made-up brand, AuraBand, says it “recharges your positive energy.” Zaki Naguib Mahmoud would ask: what test could we run to find out whether that's true or false? If no test is even possible, the sentence isn't saying anything at all.

d: The Egyptian philosopher who brought existentialism into Arabic, and believed every person is a unique existence, not a number in a crowd.
x: Abdel Rahman Badawi Damietta, Cairo and Paris, 1917–2002 Badawi was born in a village in Egypt's Nile Delta and studied philosophy at Fuad I University (today Cairo University). His 1944 doctoral thesis, Existential Time, was strongly influenced by Heidegger. His idea was that a human being isn't a fixed object like a chair; a person is an existence that unfolds in time, through choices, anxiety and freedom. What matters is the individual, not “what people say.” Beyond existentialism, he wrote, edited and translated an enormous number of books, including medieval Arabic translations of ancient Greek texts, and books on Nietzsche and others. He lived for many years in Paris and returned to Cairo a few months before his death in 2002. Someone squeezed into a packed subway car at rush hour in New York feels like nobody, one copy out of millions. Badawi would tell him: the crowd is what makes you forget you're an individual. You're not “one of the people.” You're the only one who will ever live this life of yours.

d: He said the mind is born like a blank sheet of paper, and that a government's legitimacy comes from the consent of the people.
x: John Locke England, 1632–1704 Locke is one of the most important empiricists. In An Essay Concerning Human Understanding, he argued that we aren't born with any ideas: the mind starts like a blank sheet, and experience writes on it. In politics, in his Two Treatises of Government, he said people have natural rights to life, liberty and property. People agree to form a government to protect those rights, and if the government betrays that agreement, the people have the right to replace it. He also wrote A Letter Concerning Toleration. “That kid has his dad's temper.” Locke would ask: was he born with a temper, or did he learn it in the house he grew up in? A lot of what we call “just the way he is” might actually be learned.

d: He said your freedom ends only where it harms someone else, and that the majority can be as much of a tyrant as any king.
x: John Stuart Mill London and Avignon, 1806–1873 Mill had an extremely strict upbringing: his father started teaching him Greek when he was three. Around age 20 he went through a mental crisis and came out of it convinced that feelings and art matter as much as reason. In On Liberty (1859) he proposed the harm principle: society has no right to stop you from doing something unless it harms others. He warned about the “tyranny of the majority,” meaning social pressure on anyone who's different. He also developed utilitarianism further, and in The Subjection of Women (1869) he argued for women's equality, including their right to vote. Your neighbor blasting music at 2 a.m.: that's harm, and you have every right to complain. Your neighbor dyeing his hair green: you may not like it, but it's not harm. Mill would say the difference between those two cases is the difference between freedom and babysitting.

d: He argued that many philosophical problems come from misunderstanding language, and that the meaning of a word is how it's used.
x: Ludwig Wittgenstein Vienna and Cambridge, 1889–1951 Wittgenstein's work has two phases. In the first he wrote the Tractatus Logico-Philosophicus (1921), arguing that a sentence pictures a piece of reality, and that “whereof one cannot speak, thereof one must be silent.” Then he left philosophy and worked as an elementary school teacher in rural Austrian villages. He came back with very different thinking in the Philosophical Investigations, published after his death in 1953: words don't have one fixed meaning; their meaning comes from how they're used in different “language games.” A word like “game” has no single definition covering all its uses, only a “family resemblance.” The word “fine.” From your mom, it means “I'll do it.” From your teenager, eyes glued to the phone, it can mean “leave me alone.” From your partner, in a certain tone, it means you're in trouble. Same word; the meaning is in the use.

d: The mathematician and astronomer who taught philosophy in Alexandria, drawing students from far-off places.
x: Hypatia of Alexandria Alexandria, born c. 355–370, died 415 CE Hypatia was the daughter of Theon, a mathematician in Alexandria. She taught mathematics, astronomy and Neoplatonist philosophy, and was a highly respected figure in the city. Ancient sources say she wrote commentaries on major mathematical works, like Diophantus' Arithmetica and Apollonius' Conics, but none of her writings has survived with certainty. The best source on her is the letters of her student Synesius, which show her teaching students to reason by proof and to build scientific instruments. She was killed in 415 by an angry mob, amid a political power struggle in the city. A high school student asks, “When am I ever going to use geometry?” Hypatia's tradition would answer: geometry teaches you not to believe anything until it's proven. You'll need that skill everywhere, even on a used-car lot.

d: She said one is not born a woman but becomes one: society is what writes much of the role.
x: Simone de Beauvoir Paris, 1908–1986 Beauvoir was a French existentialist philosopher and novelist. In The Second Sex (1949) she wrote her famous line: “One is not born, but rather becomes, a woman.” She meant that much of what gets called “women's nature” is really upbringing and social expectation. She argued that society treats man as the default and woman as “the Other,” defined in relation to him. In The Ethics of Ambiguity she argued that my freedom is tied to other people's freedom: I can't be truly free while I'm limiting someone else's. “Girls just naturally like cooking.” Beauvoir would ask: if it's natural, why do we have to keep teaching it and reminding them? And why are so many of the most famous restaurant chefs men?

d: She argued that great evil can be done by very ordinary people, not monsters, who simply stopped thinking.
x: Hannah Arendt Germany and New York, 1906–1975 Arendt was a German-Jewish political philosopher who fled the Nazis and settled in the United States. In The Origins of Totalitarianism (1951) she examined how totalitarian regimes take control of every part of life. In 1961 she covered the trial of Adolf Eichmann, one of the organizers of the deportation of Jews to the death camps. She expected to see a monster; she found an ordinary bureaucrat talking about “orders” and “procedures.” That gave rise to her idea of “the banality of evil” in Eichmann in Jerusalem (1963): evil can come from a person no longer thinking about what they're doing, and being unable to see the situation from anyone else's point of view. A clerk turns away an elderly woman's paperwork because “the system won't let me,” even though he knows he could fix it in two minutes, and shrugs: “I just work here.” Arendt would say that exact sentence is where the banality of evil begins.

d: Live simply and without pretense, and ask of every custom: does this actually serve me, or am I just going along with it?
x: Cynicism Greece, from the 4th century BCE It started with Antisthenes, a student of Socrates, and its most famous figure is Diogenes of Sinope. The name comes from the Greek word for “dog,” because the Cynics lived in the street and didn't care what anyone said about them. The idea: happiness means living “according to nature” and doing without money and appearances. Stories say Diogenes slept in a large storage jar and threw away his cup when he saw a child drinking from cupped hands. Those stories were written down centuries after him, so not all of them are reliable. Your brother's wedding is coming up, and everyone says you “have to” have a big venue and 300 guests, even if it means putting it on credit cards. A Cynic would ask: “Have to? Says who? And what do the two people getting married actually want?”

d: Some things are wrong even when the outcome is good, and some things are your duty even when they're not in your interest.
x: Deontology From Kant in the 18th century to today The name comes from a Greek word meaning “duty.” Instead of tallying up consequences like the utilitarians, deontology says some rules have value in themselves: don't lie, keep your promises, don't use a person as a tool. Its most famous voice is Kant. In the 20th century, W. D. Ross offered a gentler version: we have several duties, like honesty, keeping promises and preventing harm, and when two of them clash, you weigh which matters more in that situation. You promised to help your buddy move on Saturday, and on Friday night you get invited on a lake weekend. A deontologist would tell you: a promise doesn't disappear just because a better offer came along.

d: A sentence has meaning only if you can check it by experience or it's true by definition. Everything else is empty talk.
x: Logical Positivism (The Vienna Circle) Vienna, 1920s and 1930s A group of scientists and philosophers known as the Vienna Circle, including Moritz Schlick, Rudolf Carnap and Otto Neurath, published their manifesto in 1929. Influenced by the early Wittgenstein, they wanted philosophy to be as precise as science. So they said a sentence has meaning if it can be checked by observation, or if it's true by definition, like math. Anything else, including a lot of metaphysics, simply has no meaning. A. J. Ayer brought the idea to English readers in 1936, and Zaki Naguib Mahmoud brought it into Arabic. An argument at the sports bar: “This is the best pizza in Chicago.” A positivist would ask what “best” means. “Cheapest” and “sells the most pies” can be checked with numbers. “Tastes best to me” is your taste, not a fact.

d: Before you ask “What is this thing really?”, describe carefully how it shows up for you.
x: Phenomenology Germany and France, from the early 20th century Its founder was Edmund Husserl, and its famous slogan is “back to the things themselves.” Husserl built on his teacher Franz Brentano's idea that consciousness is always consciousness of something: you think about something, you're afraid of something. He proposed setting aside, for the moment, the question “Does the world really exist the way we see it?” and focusing on describing experience as we live it. He called this “bracketing.” After him, Heidegger, Sartre and Maurice Merleau-Ponty took the idea in new directions, and Merleau-Ponty focused on the body as our basic way of knowing the world. The same hour: waiting at the doctor's office for test results, it feels endless; hanging out with friends at a coffee shop, it's gone in a second. The clock on the wall is the same, but the time you live through is different, and a phenomenologist thinks that difference deserves serious study.

d: If everything has a cause before it, where is there room for your choice? And can we still hold anyone responsible?
x: Determinism and Free Will An old debate, from the Stoics to today's neuroscience This is a debate between three camps. Hard determinists: every event is the result of earlier causes, so your choice was already settled and freedom is an illusion. In 1814 Pierre-Simon Laplace imagined an intellect that knew the position of every particle and could calculate the entire future. Libertarians, in the metaphysical sense, not the political one: a person really could have chosen differently. And compatibilists, like Hume: freedom means acting on your own reasoning and desires without being forced, even if everything has a cause. In surveys of academic philosophers, compatibilism is the most common view. Your coworker blows up in a meeting and says, “That's just me, I'm hot-headed.” A hard determinist: that's the product of his upbringing and his genes. A compatibilist: nobody was holding his arm, and he can learn to calm down, so he's responsible. A libertarian: he had a real choice to stay quiet.

d: A good society starts with good people, and good people are built through ethics and courtesy in everyday dealings.
x: Confucianism China, from the 6th and 5th centuries BCE Confucius was a teacher in ancient China, and his students collected his sayings after his death in the Analects. For him, ethics is learned in everyday relationships: child and parent, student and teacher, ruler and people. Two key ideas are ren, meaning humaneness or kindness, and li, the rituals and manners that structure relationships. He's credited with the rule: “What you do not want done to yourself, do not do to others.” Later, Mencius argued that human nature is basically good, while Xunzi argued it leans toward bad and is corrected through education and ritual. You get promoted and now you manage your former coworkers. Confucius talked about “the rectification of names”: if your title is “manager,” act like a real manager. Be fair and protect your team. Trouble starts when the title says one thing and the behavior says another.

d: Morality isn't only rules and calculations. It's also seeing the person in front of you and paying attention to them.
x: Ethics of Care United States, from the 1980s Psychologist Carol Gilligan published In a Different Voice in 1982, criticizing her mentor Lawrence Kohlberg, who measured “moral maturity” by how well people applied general principles. She noticed that some people, many of them girls and women, ask a different question: Who will get hurt? How do we keep the relationship intact? She argued that this is a different voice, not a less mature one. Then in 1984 Nel Noddings wrote that the foundation of ethics is the caring relationship itself, like a parent and child or a teacher and student. Your coworker's father is in the hospital, and her part of the project is two days late. The rule says “a deadline is a deadline.” Care ethics says: before you report her, ask what she needs, and see whether you can take some of it off her plate.

d: Go back to the original sources, and learn to write, speak and think well, because education is what shapes a person.
x: Renaissance Humanism Italy, then Europe, 14th to 16th centuries During the Renaissance, scholars in Italy, Petrarch the best known among them, went back to reading ancient Greek and Latin authors like Cicero and Seneca. Their motto was ad fontes, “back to the sources”: don't rely on summaries that have passed through a hundred hands; read the original text. They championed the study of grammar, rhetoric, history, poetry and moral philosophy. In the Low Countries, Erasmus collected and explained thousands of ancient proverbs, and in 1511 published The Praise of Folly, a satire of vanity and pedantry. A post with “As the great philosopher once said…” and a million shares. A Renaissance humanist would ask: where exactly is that in his writings? Chances are the quote has been changed along the way, or made up entirely.

t: 7 Days to Stop Getting Played by Ads
d: Every ad tries to stir something in you before you think. In 7 days you'll learn the 7 most common tricks, and you'll start seeing them everywhere.
x: “Was $90, now $39.” That first number is there to be an anchor, so everything after it looks cheap. The medium popcorn at the movies isn't really there to be sold. It's there to make the large look like a deal. “Best seller” and “a million people tried it” don't tell you the product is good. They tell you a lot of people bought it. The white coat in a commercial doesn't necessarily belong to a doctor. And even if it does, that person is being paid. “95% fat-free” and “contains 5% fat” are the exact same fact. The first one just sells better. “Offer ends tonight.” “Don't miss out.” Ads scare you about losing, because a loss stings more than a gain feels good. The actor you love isn't an expert on cooking oil or banking. But your fondness for them rubs off on the product.

t: 7 Days to Win Arguments Without Being a Jerk
d: A discussion isn't a fight. In 7 days you'll learn to spot the tricks that wreck any conversation, and answer them without raising your voice.
x: Step one in any discussion: make sure you've understood the other person correctly before you respond. When someone attacks you instead of answering your point, it usually means they don't have an answer. “You're either with me or against me.” There are almost always more than two options. “Well, what about so-and-so?” moves the conversation somewhere else. A good reply: “Fair, let's talk about that later. Let's finish this first.” Whoever makes the claim has to bring the evidence. It's not your job to prove them wrong. “Well, you do it too” might be true, but it doesn't make the point itself wrong. The last lesson is the most important: someone using a fallacy doesn't mean their view is wrong. They could be right for a bad reason.

t: 7 Days to Read the News Without Panicking
d: News stories and posts scare and generalize more than reality does. In 7 days you'll learn to read any story with a calm head.
x: If the news talks about something a lot, it feels like it happens a lot. But most talked-about isn't the same as most common. Bad news grabs your attention far more than good news. That's not a flaw in you. It's a brain that evolved to survive. “My cousin had this happen” is a story, not a statistic. Stories move us, but they don't prove anything. One video of one incident says nothing about an entire group of people or a whole profession. Two things happening one after the other doesn't mean one caused the other. Anyone can pick the numbers that suit them and leave out the rest. The question is: where's the rest of the picture? We believe stories that agree with us without checking them. It's the most dangerous bias when it comes to reading the news.

d: Philosophy isn't big words in heavy books. It's questions we ask every day without noticing. In 7 days you'll meet 7 ideas that changed how humans think, and you'll try each one out in your own day.
x: Socrates didn't hand out answers. He kept asking “What do you mean by that?” until people realized they didn't understand what they thought they understood. Plato thought what we see around us might be just a shadow of a deeper reality, like people chained in a cave who see only shadows on the wall. Aristotle said virtue usually sits in the middle between two bad extremes: courage between cowardice and recklessness, generosity between stinginess and wastefulness. The Stoics split the world in two: things in your control, like your judgments and your reactions, and things outside it, like traffic and other people's opinions. Descartes decided to doubt everything he possibly could, to find a solid foundation to build on. He found that the one thing he couldn't doubt was that he was thinking, and therefore he existed. Kant proposed a test for any action: if everyone did what you're doing, would the world still work? He also said people must be treated as ends in themselves, never merely as tools. The existentialists said humans are born without a ready-made meaning, and we create ourselves through our choices. Huge freedom, and even bigger responsibility.

d: Your brain is fast and clever, but it takes shortcuts that trip it up in predictable ways. In 7 days you'll meet 7 of them and start catching them as they happen.
x: Your brain looks for whatever confirms what you already believe, and slides right past whatever contradicts it. Whatever gets talked about a lot and sticks in your head feels common, even when it's rare. When you hear a description of someone, you forget to ask: how many people like that are there in the first place? The description grabs your attention, and the base rates get forgotten. The first number you hear becomes an anchor, and every estimate after it circles around it. After something happens, you feel like you “knew it all along.” But that's your brain rewriting the memory. When someone else messes up, you think “they're careless.” When you mess up, you think “circumstances.” That's the fundamental attribution error. We credit our successes to our own skill and blame our failures on luck and other people. It protects how we feel about ourselves, but it keeps us from learning.

d: Money isn't just math. Your brain brings its biases and feelings to every money decision. In 7 days you'll learn 7 traps that drain your wallet without you noticing, from credit card rewards to “Pay in 4.” This is practice in thinking, not financial or investment advice.
x: You've already put a lot into something, so you keep going even when it's losing, so the money “isn't wasted.” But what you paid is gone either way. Losing $500 hurts more than winning $500 feels good. That can make you cling to losing bets and shy away from good decisions, like panicking every time you check your 401(k) after a bad week. “Only 3 left in stock” and “deal ends in 1 hour” make things seem more valuable, because your brain values whatever is rare. Sometimes an option is put in the middle not to be sold, but to make the pricier option look like a deal. “I've lost 5 times in a row, so I'm due for a win.” But each round is independent, and luck doesn't keep a ledger. We almost always estimate that a project will take less time and money than it really does, even when we've been through it before. The kitchen remodel that will “be done in a month” is a classic. The first result of a decision isn't the only one. Splitting a purchase into four “interest-free” payments feels easy this month, but what happens when you've stacked five of them? Always ask: “And then what?”

d: Detox teas, miracle supplements, and “the cure doctors don't want you to know about” are all over your feed. In 7 days you'll learn to spot the tricks wellness hucksters use. Important: this is practice in thinking, not medical advice. Make any decision about your health or treatment with a doctor, and never stop a medication without asking them first.
x: “100% natural” doesn't mean safe. Some plants and mushrooms are natural and poisonous. And natural products can also interact with medications you take. “My aunt tried it and got better” is a story, not a study. She may have gotten better for other reasons, and you'll never hear from the people it didn't help. People try the unusual remedy when they feel their worst. And many aches get better on their own after they peak. So the improvement gets credited to the remedy, when it was coming anyway. Two things happening one after the other doesn't mean the first caused the second. “Ever since I started wearing this bracelet, my back feels better” could be a coincidence. Someone in a white coat in a video isn't proof on their own. Ask: are they a specialist in this exact topic? And do they profit from selling the product? If a product “cures everything,” and when it doesn't work it's because “you didn't use it right,” then the claim is built so it can never be proven wrong. That's a red flag. Whoever says “this blend cures diabetes” has to bring the evidence. It's not your job to prove it doesn't. Real treatments are tested in studies before they're sold.

t: Social Media Without Getting Sucked In
d: Apps are designed to keep you scrolling. In 7 days you'll learn the tricks that hook you and the mistakes your brain makes while you scroll, and you'll be the one holding the phone again.
x: You only see the people who made it: the one who quit their job, started a business, and got rich. The one who quit and went broke doesn't make a TikTok about it. You think everyone noticed the post you deleted or the unflattering photo. In reality, everyone is busy thinking about themselves. A million likes doesn't mean something is true. It means a million people tapped a button. “You're a sensitive person but you hide it, and you have untapped potential.” That fits almost anyone, which is why personality quizzes and horoscopes feel so accurate. Upsetting posts and scary headlines grab your brain more. And the apps notice when you stop on them, so they show you more. In a group, when everyone agrees, nobody wants to be the different voice. So the whole group can follow a bad idea without anyone objecting. You bring the evidence they asked for, and they say, “No, I want something else.” It happens all the time in comment sections, and it means the argument never ends.

t: For Parents: Teach Your Kids to Think
d: Critical thinking can be learned early, through games and questions, not lectures. For 7 days, there's one simple activity a day to do with your kids at dinner or in the car. Adjust it to their age.
x: “All my friends have one” is one of the first arguments kids learn. It's a great chance to teach them that popular isn't always right. Kids connect things fast: “I wore these socks and my team won, so they're my lucky socks.” That's a great doorway to understanding cause and effect. “Boys are all annoying,” because one boy bothered your daughter. We often teach kids to generalize from one incident without meaning to. “You're just a crybaby,” instead of answering what was said. Kids do it in their fights, and so do adults. “Mom wants me to never play at all!” when you said one hour. Blowing someone's words up into a worse version is a trick that starts early. The opposite of a straw man: stating the other person's view in its best form before you respond. It's a skill that teaches kids to listen before they fight. The most important lesson: changing your mind when new evidence comes in isn't losing, it's smart. Kids learn this by watching their parents do it.

d: Good scientists, engineers, and detectives carry a toolbox for thinking: simple tools that save them from a lot of trouble. In 7 days you'll pick up 7 tools and try each one on a real situation from your day.
x: Occam's razor: if there are two explanations, start with the simpler one that needs fewer assumptions. That doesn't mean it's always right. It means it's the first one to test. The power went out in your building? Probably a fault, not a plot by the neighbors. Hanlon's razor: don't blame on bad intent what can be explained by oversight or carelessness. Your friend didn't answer your text? They're probably busy, not mad at you. Before you answer a view, state it in its strongest form, one its holder would agree with. If you can answer that strong version, your answer is worth something. Chesterton's fence: if you find a fence in the middle of a road and don't know why it's there, don't tear it down until you find out. There may be an important reason you can't see. The idea comes from a 1929 book by the English writer G. K. Chesterton. Instead of asking “How do I succeed?”, flip the question: “What would guarantee that I fail?” Then avoid it. Working backward sometimes shows you what you've been missing. The first result is obvious, but what comes after it? Raising your prices earns you more today, but your customers might go elsewhere next month. Ask “And then what?” twice. Before you start any project, imagine it's 6 months later and it failed completely, then ask: what happened? This exercise surfaces problems nobody would have dared to mention.
